chapters.title: Chapter 5: Tax, Tracking, and Your Deal Checklist

lessons.title: How Mergers, Buyouts, and Demergers Are Taxed for Shareholders

children.text: Every corporate action in this course ends in the same place: your income tax return. The good news is that Indian tax law treats most mergers and demergers as reorganisations rather than sales, so nothing is taxed when your shares convert. The trap is that something usually is taxable somewhere, whether it is the cash you receive for a fraction of a share, the shares you tender in an open offer, or the buyback cheque that is no longer tax-free. This lesson sorts every deal event in the course into taxable and not taxable, and shows you what to report.

body.text: Conversion is not a sale. Cash is. If a deal hands you shares, tax usually waits until you sell them, and your original cost and purchase date travel with you. If a deal hands you money, tax arrives that year.

children.text: Why Mergers and Demergers Escape Tax
Capital gains are charged under section 67 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (section 45 of the 1961 Act) only when there is a
transfer

of a capital asset. Section 70 of the 2025 Act (section 47 of the 1961 Act) lists transactions that are not regarded as transfers, and both qualifying mergers and qualifying demergers are on that list, as long as the surviving or resulting company is an Indian company and shareholders are paid in shares.

markDefs.definition: Defined in section 2(109) of the 2025 Act (section 2(47) of the 1961 Act). It includes sale, exchange, relinquishment and the extinguishment of rights in an asset, which is why an exemption is needed for merger conversions.

children.text: Two further rules make the exemption work properly when you eventually sell.
Cost carries over.
Under section 73 of the 2025 Act (section 49 of the 1961 Act), the cost of your new shares is the cost of the old ones, split proportionately in a demerger as Lesson 4.3 showed.
Holding period carries over.
Under section 2(101) of the 2025 Act (section 2(42A) of the 1961 Act), the time you held the original shares counts towards the holding period of the new ones.

body.text: This is a deferral, not a waiver. The tax you did not pay on conversion is still sitting in your holding, because your cost stayed at the old, lower figure. When you finally sell, the gain covers the whole period you held both the old and the new shares.

children.text: Worked Example: An HDFC Ltd Shareholder Sells
Deepak bought 100 HDFC Ltd shares at ₹2,200 in 2021, a total cost of ₹2,20,000. In the 2023 merger he received 168 HDFC Bank shares at 42 for every 25. He paid no tax then.

body.title: Deepak's carried-over cost
body.prompt: Deepak's ₹2,20,000 cost now attaches to 168 HDFC Bank shares. What is his cost per HDFC Bank share, in rupees? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: ₹2,20,000 ÷ 168 = ₹1,309.52 per share. Nothing about his total cost changed. It simply spread across more shares, because he received more shares than he gave up.

body.title: The gain when he sells
body.prompt: Deepak sells all 168 HDFC Bank shares at ₹1,700 each. What is his capital gain, in rupees? Ignore brokerage and other charges.
body.explanation: Sale value = 168 × ₹1,700 = ₹2,85,600. Gain = ₹2,85,600 minus ₹2,20,000 = ₹65,600. Because his holding period runs from 2021, it is long-term. If this is his only long-term listed equity gain in the tax year, it sits below the ₹1.25 lakh exemption, so no tax is payable.

body.title: Tax on an open offer tender
body.prompt: Ravi bought 200 shares at ₹300 and tendered all 200 in an open offer at ₹465, eight months later. The offer was oversubscribed and only 100 of his shares were accepted. Ignoring cess and surcharge, how much tax does he owe on the accepted shares, in rupees?
body.explanation: Gain on accepted shares = 100 × (₹465 minus ₹300) = ₹16,500. He held them for eight months, so this is short-term and taxed at 20% under section 196 of the 2025 Act (section 111A of the 1961 Act): ₹16,500 × 20% = ₹3,300, plus cess. His other 100 shares came back to his demat account, and nothing is taxable on them until he sells.

body.text: The ₹1.25 lakh exemption applies to your total long-term listed equity gains for the whole tax year, not to each sale. A large open offer or a merger-related sale can use up the entire exemption in one go, making other gains that year fully taxable.

children.text: Buybacks: The Rule That Changed

body.title: Buyback taxation before and after 1 October 2024

columns.label: Up to 30 September 2024
points: The company paid a buyback tax
Proceeds were exempt in the shareholder's hands
Tendering in a buyback was often more tax-efficient than selling in the market

columns.label: From 1 October 2024
points: The company no longer pays buyback tax
The entire amount you receive is taxed as dividend income at your slab rate
Your cost of those shares becomes a capital loss you can set off against capital gains
High slab-rate investors may prefer selling in the market instead

body.label: A buyback example under the current rule
body.context: If you bought 100 shares at ₹200 and the company buys them back at ₹500, the full ₹50,000 is taxed as dividend income at your slab rate, and the ₹20,000 cost becomes a capital loss available for set-off against capital gains, subject to the usual rules.

body.title: Which event is taxable this year?
body.question: During one tax year, Sneha received HDFC Bank shares when HDFC Ltd merged, received ITC Hotels shares in the demerger, received ₹180 in cash for a fractional entitlement, and had 50 shares accepted in an open offer at a profit. Which of these creates taxable income this year?
options: All four, because she received something in each case
Only the merger and demerger, because new shares have value
Only the fractional entitlement cash and the open offer tender
None, because corporate actions are always tax-neutral
body.explanation: The merger and demerger conversions are not transfers, so nothing is taxable until she sells those shares. Cash for a fractional entitlement is a sale of that fraction, and the open offer tender is a straightforward sale of shares. Both must be reported this year, even though the fractional amount is tiny.

body.title: The annual shield
body.textWithBlank: Long-term capital gains on listed equity are taxed at 12.5% only above ₹___ lakh of such gains in a tax year.
body.explanation: The exemption is ₹1.25 lakh of long-term listed equity gains per tax year, applied across all such gains, not per transaction.

children.text: Shares bought before 1 February 2018.

For long-term gains on listed equity acquired before that date, the cost can be stepped up to the fair market value as on 31 January 2018, subject to limits, under section 90 of the 2025 Act (section 55(2)(ac) of the 1961 Act). If those shares later went through a merger or demerger, the stepped-up figure is what carries over or gets split.
Company-level tax rules are not yours.

Provisions that let an amalgamated company carry forward the accumulated losses of the company it absorbed, subject to conditions, apply to the companies, not to shareholders. They matter to you only through their effect on the combined company's profits.
Off-market sales lose the concessional route.

Section 198 of the 2025 Act (section 112A) applies to listed equity sold on a stock exchange with STT paid. A sale outside the exchange, such as selling to an acquirer in the exit window after delisting, falls under other provisions, and unlisted shares need 24 months rather than 12 to qualify as long-term.

body.title: One busy tax year
body.scenario: Anil's tax year includes four deal events. His shares in a company he held for three years were converted in a merger, and he still holds the new shares. He received ₹212 in cash for a fractional entitlement. He tendered 300 shares in an open offer at ₹880 against a cost of ₹640, held for five years, and all 300 were accepted. And he sold the demerger shares he received two years ago in another company for ₹1,40,000, with a split cost of ₹38,000.
body.prompt: What must Anil report, and roughly what tax will he pay? Ignore cess and surcharge.
body.modelAnswer:
1. The merger conversion: nothing to report as income. He keeps records of his original cost and purchase date for when he eventually sells.
2. Fractional entitlement: ₹212 is a sale of a fraction. The gain is small but should be reported in the capital gains schedule.
3. Open offer: 300 × (₹880 minus ₹640) = ₹72,000 long-term gain, since he held for five years.
4. Demerger shares sold: ₹1,40,000 minus ₹38,000 = ₹1,02,000 long-term gain, using the split cost from Lesson 4.3 and the original purchase date.
5. Total long-term listed equity gains = ₹72,000 + ₹1,02,000 = ₹1,74,000, plus the small fractional gain. After the ₹1.25 lakh exemption, about ₹49,000 is taxable at 12.5%, roughly ₹6,125 before cess.
6. Records to keep: the scheme documents, the cost apportionment announcement, contract notes and the open offer acceptance letter. His broker statements may show zero or unsplit costs, so he should file on his own corrected figures.

body.title: Tax paperwork for any deal
steps: Note which events gave you shares and which gave you cash
Record the original purchase date and cost of the shares involved
Apply the company's cost apportionment announcement for any demerger
Collect contract notes, acceptance letters and fractional entitlement credits
Check your Annual Information Statement and broker tax report against your own figures
Track your total long-term listed equity gains for the year against the ₹1.25 lakh exemption
Keep the scheme documents with your tax papers for the years you hold the shares

body.description: Read the official text of the Income-tax Act, 2025 and its section mapping, and check your Annual Information Statement for how brokers reported your deal transactions.

cards.definition: Not a transfer under section 70 of the 2025 Act (section 47 of the 1961 Act). No tax when your shares convert.
Section 73 of the 2025 Act (section 49 of the 1961 Act). Your old cost becomes the cost of the new shares.
Section 2(101) of the 2025 Act (section 2(42A) of the 1961 Act). Time held before the deal still counts.
20% under section 196 of the 2025 Act (section 111A of the 1961 Act) for holdings of 12 months or less.
12.5% under section 198 of the 2025 Act (section 112A of the 1961 Act) on gains above ₹1.25 lakh a year.
Taxable as a sale of the fractional share, however small the amount.
The full amount received is taxed as dividend income at your slab rate, and the cost becomes a capital loss.

points: Receiving shares in a qualifying merger or demerger is not a transfer, so no tax arises on conversion.
Your cost and holding period carry over, which defers tax rather than removing it.
Cash is taxable: fractional entitlements, open offer tenders, delisting tenders and squeeze-outs are all sales.
Listed equity sold on an exchange is taxed at 20% short-term under section 196 (111A) and 12.5% long-term above ₹1.25 lakh under section 198 (112A).
Since 1 October 2024, buyback proceeds are taxed as dividend income at your slab rate, with the cost allowed as a capital loss.
Keep the scheme documents, cost apportionment announcements and contract notes, because broker statements often carry wrong costs after a deal.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not tax, legal or investment advice. Section references are to the Income-tax Act, 2025 as in force for tax year 2026-27, with corresponding 1961 Act sections in brackets, and the correspondence of specific sub-sections should be confirmed against the official text. Rates, exemption limits and conditions change, and transfers before 1 April 2026 are governed by the 1961 Act. Deepak, Ravi, Sneha and Anil are fictional, and share prices used are illustrative. Consult a qualified chartered accountant for your own situation.
